Ophthalmology · published research

Amblyopia

A partially sham-controlled adult study reported visual-acuity improvement in about 90% of treated eyes, maintained for at least six months. A 66-child randomized study reported faster acuity improvement with red-light treatment added to spectacles over six weeks; a case report is uncontrolled.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A partially sham-controlled adult study reported visual-acuity improvement in about 90% of treated eyes, maintained for at least six months. A 66-child randomized study reported faster acuity improvement with red-light treatment added to spectacles over six weeks; a case report is uncontrolled.

Summary of the Evidence

Four unique titles were identified: two controlled human studies, one human case report, and one review. The primary studies concern different age groups and amblyopia subtypes, and no shared cohort was identified. The review summarizes existing reports and is not an additional trial.

Human and clinical evidence

Ivandic and Ivandic retrospectively studied adolescents and adults with amblyopia, with a partially sham-controlled subgroup. They reported visual-acuity improvement in about 90% of treated eyes, including gains of three or more lines in many eyes, with the effect maintained for at least six months; the control group showed no comparable change. Li and colleagues randomized 66 children aged four to eight with myopic amblyopia to spectacles alone or spectacles plus repeated low-level red light. The combination group had faster visual-acuity improvement and less axial elongation over six weeks. A 2026 report describes one child with high myopic anisometropic amblyopia and is a case report, not a controlled result (Ivandic & Ivandic 2012 Li et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory evidence was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The adult study used 780 nm near-infrared laser exposure over two weeks, with a reported total fluence of 0.77 J/cm². The pediatric study used 650 nm red light at 2 J per treatment, twice daily for six weeks, alongside spectacles. Differences in age, amblyopia type, comparator, and regimen limit direct comparison; the short pediatric follow-up does not establish durable benefit.

Interpretation

The studies report visual-acuity improvement in their specific populations, but the evidence does not show a common effect across amblyopia types or establish long-term benefit from one standardized regimen.

Evidence strength in source summaryVisual acuity in myopic amblyopia: Low Durable benefit across amblyopia types: Very low
Publications and records4 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One partial-sham retrospective study in adults and adolescents and one small randomized pediatric comparison report visual-acuity gains, but populations and protocols differ. A case report adds no controlled estimate, and the only randomized trial lasted six weeks. Independent trials with sham or standard-care controls and longer follow-up are needed.
